title: A hymn in Maru
hookLine: Maru holds the long Solhe and Kabir's song of the true warrior

cards: A drum sounds in the sky. A target is struck. A fighter has stepped onto the field, and the poem says: now is the time to fight.
That's how a verse begins near the end of Raga Maru, and the voice isn't a general's. It's Kabir, the weaver-poet whose verses the Gurus gathered into the Granth.
Maru also holds the long Solhe, great extended hymns of the Gurus. But today, Kabir's battlefield, and the kind of warrior he means.

teach.h: THE DRUM SOUNDS; THE FIELD IS SET.
teach.b: Here's Kabir, in plain English, not word for word.

teach.h: THE BATTLE IN THE MIND'S SKY.
teach.b: The battle drum sounds in the sky; the target is struck. The warrior has entered the field; now is the time to fight.
Then the lines at its heart: the true warrior is the one who fights for the sake of the deen, and who, even cut apart piece by piece, never leaves the field. Two things are worth hearing closely.

First, the drum in the sky. Some readers hear that sky as the inner sky of the mind, where Kabir's battle is fought: against ego, greed, fear and the rest. The poem sounds like a battlefield and points inward.
Some translators give it as the poor and helpless, so the true warrior fights for the defenseless. Others give it as faith, or the path of righteousness.
Both readings have their commentators, and the hymn bears them both. Either way, he isn't fighting for glory, plunder or a grudge, but for something beyond himself.
And what makes him a warrior isn't winning. It's staying. Cut apart, he doesn't leave the field.
Some Sikhs connect this verse to the ideal of the saint-soldier, a person of prayer who is also ready to stand up for others. Yesterday's courage was without fear and without hate.
Kabir gives it a body and a place to stand: in the field, for the deen, all the way through.
That's today's line: the true warrior.

how: Kabir's hymn of the true warrior is sung in kirtan in Raga Maru, and its closing lines are quoted by some Sikhs when speaking of the saint-soldier ideal of the Khalsa.

games.q: what does “a hymn in maru” mean?
o: a hymn praising the bravest general of the Sikh army
a victory song sung after the army has won the battle
Kabir's verse of the true warrior who never leaves the field

games.q: what's inside the hymn — tap the pairs.
p: the helpless, or the right path

s: Kabir's true warrior is the one who wins
the mark of the warrior is staying: even cut apart, he never leaves the field.
translators give the word deen more than one meaning
some say the poor and helpless, others faith or the right path.
the hymn is a general's war song
it's Kabir's, and some readers hear its sky as the inner sky of the mind.

games.q: you're the warrior in Kabir's hymn. the drum has sounded and the fight is going badly. what does the hymn say the true warrior does?
o: stays on the field, whatever it costs.
fights on only if victory is certain.
games.why: Kabir: cut apart piece by piece, the true warrior never leaves the field, fighting for the deen, the helpless or the right.

practice: Sit with your feet down and your back steady, and notice the first thing that pulls you away: an itch, a thought, a plan for later.
Each time the mind leaves, don't fight it angrily; see where it went and come back to the breath, as calmly as a soldier returning to post, leaving and returning without a grudge.
If you pray, say Waheguru each time you return; if you don't, simply say back, silently.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Maru. Kabir's song of the true warrior, who fights for the deen, the helpless or the right, and never leaves the field. Today's word.

orig.note: sura, warrior, hero: Kabir's word for the one who never leaves the field.

carryVoice: Your line: the true warrior. In Kabir's verse, the warrior is the one who stays. See you tomorrow.
